issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Situations: Sexual situations or intimacy
issues.explanation: For a 42-year-old married male ship captain with a man-made disaster trauma, 'sexual situations or intimacy' is a hard-to-explain trigger unless the disaster had a sexual/interpersonal component, which is not suggested anywhere else in the profile. The other trigger items (object throwing, uniforms) fit danger/aggression themes, making this item stand out as clinically incongruent with the trauma context.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Sexual Coping: I release my tension with sexual fantasies/ activities
issues.explanation: 'Sexual coping' appears to be organized around the same sexualized theme as the sexual trigger, but that theme is otherwise absent from Threat, Negative Appraisals, and the disaster trauma context. In this profile it does not cohere with the dominant formulation of external danger, mistrust, and vigilance, whereas dropping responsibilities and gambling are more plausibly linked to avoidance/arousal management.

vignette:
Marcus Chen

Marcus Chen had been captain of the Pacific Star for sixteen years, a 280-foot container vessel that ran regular routes between Long Beach and Shanghai. He loved the ocean, loved the clarity of command, the weight of responsibility that came with knowing four hundred million dollars of cargo and a crew of twenty depended on his decisions. That love ended on a Tuesday afternoon in March when a disgruntled former crew member, turned away at the gangway, returned with a pipe bomb. The device detonated near the bridge during afternoon watch, killing two of Marcus's officers instantly and shattering the windows of the wheelhouse. Marcus himself was thrown backward, his shoulder dislocated, his hearing temporarily gone. What stayed with him longer than the physical injuries was the moment just before the explosion-a sound like a door slamming, then nothing, then the world tilting sideways. The man who planted the bomb was arrested within hours. He served four years and was released two years ago on a legal technicality. Marcus read about it in a maritime newsletter. No one had asked Marcus's opinion. No one seemed to think it mattered.

In the months after the blast, Marcus had tried to return to work. His company offered him a shore-based position-administrative, safe, landlocked. He refused it. He was a ship's captain; the sea was his life. But within weeks of resuming command, he found himself unable to trust his crew. They were competent, loyal, many of them the same men who'd been aboard that day, yet Marcus had come to believe he could not rely on other people, not really, not when it mattered. Someone could always turn on you. Someone could walk away one day and return with violence. This certainty had hardened into something unshakeable. The thought that he might be wrong, that he might be able to trust again, felt impossibly dangerous-if he lowered his guard and someone hurt his crew, he would not survive it. Better to assume the worst and be ready.

That assumption began to reshape his days. Marcus found himself hypervigilant for dangerous people on the dock, studying the faces of vendors and port officials with an intensity that made others uncomfortable. He started choosing which crew members could access the bridge, which could be near the fuel lines. He positioned himself always with his back to a wall, always able to see the exits. When they were in port, he would not leave the ship. When he had to be ashore, he avoided unfamiliar places entirely-he could not assess the danger in new territory, could not control the variables, and the uncertainty itself felt like a threat. His wife, Sarah, asked him to attend her company holiday party in a hotel ballroom downtown. He declined. He chose a table at the back of restaurants, never the center, never anywhere he felt exposed. At night, he lay awake beside Sarah, unable to fall asleep because he needed to stay alert, to listen for sounds that didn't belong, to keep watch. His mind would race through scenarios: a fire at the dock, an intruder on deck, an accident he hadn't foreseen. Sleep felt like surrender.

Within six months, Marcus had given up the shore-based administrative role he'd briefly accepted-a decision that baffled his company, but he couldn't bear being in an office where he couldn't see the exits, couldn't monitor the hallways. He dropped his involvement in the maritime union's safety committee, a position he'd held proudly for a decade. He stopped attending his daughter's soccer games because the field was too open, too exposed, and he couldn't position himself safely. Each responsibility he shed felt necessary, a calculation of risk versus safety, yet each one also confirmed his deepest fear: that he was becoming someone unreliable, someone who couldn't show up for the people who needed him. That fear fed his sense that others couldn't rely on him either, which made his conviction that he couldn't rely on them feel even more justified. If he was failing them, surely they would fail him.

To manage the creeping dread, Marcus began gambling. A casino forty minutes from home became a place he could go-enclosed, controlled, with clear exits and security cameras he could see. The noise and stimulation there distracted him from the constant scanning, the endless vigilance. He told Sarah it was a stress release, a way to unwind, but it was more than that. It was permission to stop thinking, to let his mind go blank in the rush of placing bets and watching the reels spin. He lost seven thousand dollars in three months. When Sarah found the credit card statements, she wept. He couldn't explain it in a way that made sense to her, couldn't articulate that the gambling was the only time he didn't feel like he was failing everyone, the only time he could escape the loop of hypervigilance and shame.

Then, last month, a police officer came aboard during a routine port inspection. His uniform-navy blue, badge, the weight of authority-triggered something visceral in Marcus. He found himself unable to stay in the room. He left the bridge, his hands shaking, his breath shallow. Later, when a container fell on the dock and made a sound like an explosion, Marcus flinched so violently he nearly fell. His crew noticed. Word would get back to the company. He was unraveling, and he knew it.

What frightened Marcus most now was the thought that if he allowed himself to think about the bombing, to really think about it, he would not be able to handle it-that he would fall apart entirely and there would be no coming back. So he didn't think about it. He pushed it away, kept moving, kept scanning, kept gambling, kept avoiding. But the avoidance was becoming its own trap. He was missing his life. Sarah had stopped asking him to come home early. His daughter had stopped inviting him to games. And somewhere in that silence, Marcus had begun to wonder if the man who planted the bomb had already won-not with the explosion, but with this: the slow erosion of everything that made him who he was. It was this thought, finally, that made him call a therapist. He needed to know if there was any way back, or if he was truly alone in this, as he had come to believe.
